title: Introduction to C++ Programming
learningObjectives: Define C++ as a general-purpose programming language.
Identify common application areas of C++.
Recognize procedural, object-oriented and generic programming styles.
Explain C++'s combination of abstractions and low-level control.
Describe why correctness and safe resource practices matter when using C++.

understand.concept: C++ is a general-purpose compiled programming language used in desktop software, games, embedded systems, simulations, developer tools and performance-sensitive applications. It supports procedural programming, object-oriented design and generic programming. It offers high-level abstractions while allowing detailed control over data and resources.
understand.whyItMatters: C++ is useful where performance, control, reusable abstractions or mature libraries matter. Its flexibility also means programmers must pay attention to correctness, object lifetimes and resource management.
understand.analogy: C++ is like a toolbox with both simple tools and advanced tools for building reusable systems; you choose the tool suited to the task.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not capture language standards, type rules, compiler behaviour or undefined behaviour.
understand.explain:
## C++ in brief
C++ builds on ideas from C and adds facilities such as classes, templates, exceptions and a rich standard library. It is not restricted to one application type.

## Programming styles
Procedural code organizes tasks into functions. Object-oriented code uses classes and objects to combine state and behaviour. Generic programming uses templates to express reusable operations for compatible types. C++ programs often combine these styles.

## Typical applications
C++ is used in game engines, desktop apps, simulations, embedded software, browsers, tools and systems where resource control or performance matters.

## Trade-offs
C++ does not automatically make code fast or safe. Poor algorithms, invalid memory access, lifetime mistakes and unchecked input can cause defects. Prefer clear design, standard library features and testing.

examples.title: Basic arithmetic
examples.code: #include <iostream>\nint main() { int x = 8, y = 5; std::cout << x + y << '\\n'; }
examples.explanation: Two integer values are added and printed.

examples.title: Reusable function
examples.code: #include <iostream>\nint square(int n) { return n * n; }\nint main() { std::cout << square(4) << '\\n'; }
examples.explanation: The square function names a reusable calculation.

examples.title: Class example
examples.code: #include <iostream>\nclass Counter { public: int value=0; void increment(){ ++value; } };\nint main(){ Counter c; c.increment(); std::cout << c.value << '\\n'; }
examples.explanation: A class can combine data with operations; public data is used here for simplicity.

examples.title: Standard container
examples.explanation: The vector container stores a sequence and reports its element count.

examples.title: Generic template
examples.code: #include <iostream>\ntemplate<class T> T bigger(T a,T b){ return a>b?a:b; }\nint main(){ std::cout << bigger(3,7) << '\\n'; }
examples.explanation: A template lets a reusable function work with compatible types.

practise.guidedTask: Trace Example 1, predict the output, change one value, and predict again. Verify with a compiler if available.
practise.independentTask: Create a small program that calculates a shopping total. Refactor the calculation into a function and compare the two versions.
hints: The standard library provides containers and utilities.
Compile and test; a successful build is not proof of correct logic.
